# SaintsTombs.com: UX Engineering, Frontend Architecture, and Digital Humanities Case Study > **Live Application:** [saintstombs.com](https://saintstombs.com) · **Source Repository:** [github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs) > **Role:** End-to-End Owner (Product Strategy, Information Architecture, Design Systems, Frontend & Edge Engineering, Custom CMS & Data Pipeline) > **Stack:** React 19 · TypeScript 5.9 · Vite 8 · React Router 7 · Marked · Gray Matter · Cloudflare Pages & Workers (`_worker.js`) · GitHub Contents API --- ## Overview **SaintsTombs.com** is an open-access digital pilgrimage gazetteer and hagiographical index that maps **14,290 indexed holy figures** across **5,824 shrines, churches, and towns** in **138 countries** on six continents. The project came to me as a commission from a parishioner who has spent more than twenty years, going all the way back to 2003, hand-collecting this data by reading through books and traveling to many of these places himself. His ask was pretty humble: he wanted his decades of work out in the open where people could actually use it, along with a simple place for visitors to send him a tip if they found it helpful. That goal shaped every technical decision I made. I wanted to make his data as useful as possible to travelers and researchers while keeping his handmade notes as the true source of truth. To pull that off, I modernized the site from a multi-page vanilla HTML setup and an early third-party CMS and database prototype into a **zero-database, edge-cached React 19 and TypeScript app** paired with a **custom Git-backed Structured Markdown CMS** on Cloudflare Pages Workers. That setup gives people **sub-millisecond client-side filtering (`0.62 ms` p50)**, a **`75.48 KB` gzipped** initial JavaScript payload, thoughtful keyboard and screen-reader support, and a lossless editing workflow that keeps his scholarly notes intact across **57,282 lines** of structured Markdown. --- ## 1. The User Problem, Information Architecture, and End-to-End Ownership ### 1.1 The Problem Space This project sits at the intersection of two real-world problems: respecting the craft of the person who built the archive, and making decades of scattered burial records easy to search for everyone else. First up is the creator's side of the equation. The parishioner who commissioned this site didn't compile these records with a software schema in mind. He spent decades pouring through history books, checking references, and exploring churches and shrines in person, recording everything in his own careful, handmade notes. He wasn't looking to maintain a complicated backend or become a database administrator. He simply wanted to share what he had gathered so other people could benefit from it, and give appreciative visitors an easy way to send him a tip (handled via the `/donate` page) if the site proved useful on a trip or research project. Any architecture that locked his notes inside a proprietary database, or forced him to flatten his nuanced historical asides into rigid form fields, would have worked against the entire point of the project. His handmade files had to stay the authoritative source of truth. Meanwhile, on the visitor side, anyone trying to track down historical Christian burial sites faces a fragmented discovery problem. Reliable burial data for saints, blesseds, venerables, and Servants of God is spread across regional diocesan booklets, out-of-print martyrologies, and aging web forums. People who end up looking for this information usually fall into one of two camps, and existing tools tend to leave both of them hanging: 1. **On-the-Road & Route-Based Pilgrimage (Geographic-First):** Picture a traveler driving down Italy's Autostrada A24 near *Tagliacozzo*, or standing inside an old parish church in a European city, wondering if a saint is buried nearby, which chapel or cemetery holds the tomb, and whether a feast day (*dies natalis*, which for those less familiar is the traditional liturgical term for a saint's date of death) lines up with their visit. Classic references like *Butler's Lives of the Saints*, Wikipedia, and *CatholicSaints.info* are great for what they are, but they are indexed alphabetically by **person**. That makes sense in a printed encyclopedia, sure, yet it makes geographic lookup on a phone almost impossible. 2. **Hagiographical & Prosopographical Research (Entity-First):** Historians, diocesan archivists, and digital humanists come in with a completely different set of questions. For those who haven't run into the term, prosopography is the study of historical groups through shared biographical details. These researchers need to cross-reference canonical status (*Servant of God*, *Venerable*, *Blessed*, *Saint*), religious order post-nominals (`OFM`, `OSB`, `SJ`, `O.Cart.`), relic provenance versus full bodily interment, and historical uncertainty across borders that have shifted over two thousand years. ### 1.2 Information Architecture To serve both kinds of visitors without breaking the underlying structure of the author's notes, I designed a **dual-access Information Architecture** powered by a single 4-tier geographic-hagiographical taxonomy: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Source["Canonical Markdown Gazetteer (19 Regional Files · 57,282 Lines)"] direction TB L1["Tier 1: Region / Country (# H1)"] L2["Tier 2: Town & Admin Unit (Alphabetical)"] L3["Tier 3: Church, Shrine, Cemetery, or '???' (- Bullet)"] L4["Tier 4: Holy Figure Record (Nested Bullet: Rank, Name/Aliases, Order, Role, Feast/Death Date, Provenance)"] L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 end subgraph Discovery["Dual User Discovery Paths"] direction TB P1["Entity-First Faceted Search (/saints & ⌘K Modal)
Free-text query + Continent → Country cascading filters"] P2["Corridor-First Regional Gazetteer (/regions)
Alphabetical towns + auto-generated 'Jump to Country' TOC"] end subgraph Curation["Scholarly Stewardship Loop"] direction TB C1["Public Peer Corrections (/contact → Formspree)"] C2["Authenticated Editorial CMS (/admin → GitHub OAuth)"] end Source -->|"Build-Time JSON Indexer"| P1 Source -->|"On-Demand Markdown Fetch + Marked"| P2 C1 --> C2 -->|"Atomic Git Commit"| Source ``` A few deliberate UX and IA choices hold this together: - **First up, cascading geographic facets:** Countries packed with entries (Italy, Spain, France, Germany, Britain) get their own dedicated regional gazetteers. Smaller or more dispersed territories are grouped regionally (like *Eastern Europe*, *Latin America*, and *Oceania*) with an auto-generated **Jump to Country** anchor table of contents (`buildToc` in [RegionsPage.tsx](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/pages/RegionsPage.tsx#L34-L42)) so multi-country pages stay easy to scan. - **Quick global search from anywhere (`⌘K` / `Ctrl+K`):** If you are halfway down a long list on `/regions` or reading `/about`, you can pop open the lazy-loaded [GlobalSearchModal.tsx](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/components/GlobalSearchModal.tsx) with a keyboard shortcut or the floating glassmorphic pill in the corner, look someone up, and jump right back without losing your scroll position. - **Another meaningful addition is ambient liturgical theming:** I didn't want the visual palette to feel like arbitrary branding, so [liturgicalTheme.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/utils/liturgicalTheme.ts) implements the **Meeus/Jones/Butcher Gregorian Easter computus** right in the browser. (For those that don't know, a *computus* is the traditional astronomical calculation used to pin down the date of Easter each year.) Using that calculation, the site quietly shifts its CSS custom properties (`data-liturgical-color`) with the Church calendar: Green for Ordinary Time, Purple for Advent and Lent, White for Christmas, the Triduum, and Easter, Red for Passion Sunday and Pentecost, and Rose for Gaudete and Laetare Sundays. It even handles midnight rollovers automatically and remembers manual overrides in `localStorage`. ### 1.3 End-to-End Ownership | Discipline | Owned Deliverables | | --- | --- | | **Product & IA** | Client discovery with the archive's author, persona modeling (on-road pilgrims and DH researchers), 4-tier gazetteer taxonomy, progressive result disclosure (`24` cards/page), peer-correction flow, and tip/support page (`/donate`). | | **Design System & Accessibility** | Dark glassmorphic UI built on CSS custom properties, seasonal liturgical palettes, `Texturina` editorial serif typography, WCAG-conscious skip links, focus traps, ARIA live regions, and responsive mobile drawers. | | **Frontend Engineering** | Migration from vanilla multi-page HTML/JS to **React 19 + TypeScript 5.9 + Vite 8**, route-level code splitting, React 19 `useDeferredValue` search handling, and `Intl.Collator` diacritic-insensitive Unicode sorting. | | **Edge & CMS Engineering** | Custom **Cloudflare Pages Worker** ([worker/index.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/worker/index.ts)) handling GitHub OAuth 2.0, `HttpOnly` session cookies, repo push-permission verification, and optimistic-concurrency Git commits; custom bidirectional Markdown AST parser/serializer ([regionsParser.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/utils/regionsParser.ts), [regionsSerializer.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/utils/regionsSerializer.ts)). | | **Build & Data Pipeline** | Multi-schema Markdown-to-JSON compiler ([build-saints-index.mjs](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/scripts/build-saints-index.mjs)), automated round-trip fidelity test harness ([test-roundtrip.mjs](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/scripts/test-roundtrip.mjs)), and Wrangler edge deployment pipeline. | --- ## 2. 0.62 ms p50 Filter · 24-Card Windowing"] RegionsUI["/regions Gazetteer
Lazy-loaded Marked Renderer + Dynamic TOC"] end Editor -->|"Prod: PUT + Blob SHA"| EdgeWorker Editor -->|"Dev: PUT"| LocalVite EdgeWorker -->|"GitHub Contents API Commit"| GitHub GitHub -->|"Build Trigger"| Indexer Indexer --> JSONOut --> ViteBuild --> CDN Esbuild --> CDN CDN --> Browser Browser --> SearchUI Browser --> RegionsUI ``` ### 2.2 How the Architecture Evolved (and Why) Every choice below comes back to the same constraint: squeeze maximum utility out of this dataset for visitors without ever taking control away from the parishioner's handmade Markdown notes. #### Trade-Off 1: Replacing Cloudflare D1 (SQLite FTS5) Search with a Build-Time Static Index An earlier version of the project ([content/source-repo/workers/search/schema.sql](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/content/source-repo/workers/search/schema.sql)) prototyped a serverless search API built on **Cloudflare D1 and SQLite FTS5** virtual tables with sync triggers. On paper, that is a very respectable setup: FTS5 gives you BM25 ranking and stemming out of the box. In practice, though, it fought against keeping the handmade notes as the true source of truth: - **Index Drift:** Every Markdown edit meant running `node populate.js > /tmp/seed.sql` and pushing remote D1 migrations, leaving awkward windows where live search results fell out of sync with the Git source files. - **Per-Keystroke Network Latency:** Every search query paid for an edge Worker invocation, CORS preflight overhead, and a D1 lookup. That lag really shows up when a traveler is searching over spotty European cellular service. **What I ended up building instead:** At build time, [build-saints-index.mjs](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/scripts/build-saints-index.mjs) compiles all 19 Markdown files directly into two static CDN files (`saints.json` and `filters.json`). In the browser, [useSaintSearch.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/hooks/useSaintSearch.ts) caches one module-level `dataPromise` (so `/saints` and `GlobalSearchModal` share the same fetch), pre-computes a lowercase `normalizedSearchText` field per record, sorts names cleanly with a diacritic-insensitive `Intl.Collator`, and wraps filtering in React 19's `useDeferredValue` so typing stays crisp. | Dimension | Legacy D1 + FTS5 Edge API | Current Static Index + Client Deferred Search | | --- | --- | --- | | **Source-of-Truth Parity** | Async manual re-seeding (`populate.js`) | Guaranteed atomic parity on every `prebuild` | | **Keystroke Latency (Post-Load)** | Network RTT + Worker + D1 query (~40 to 250 ms) | **0.62 ms p50 / 1.42 ms p99** in-memory V8 scan | | **Offline / Weak-Signal Resilience** | Fails without live network per query | Full search & facet filtering works offline once cached | | **Initial Data Payload** | Minimal per query (~5 to 20 KB) | `661.7 KB` gzip / `404.3 KB` brotli one-time transfer | | **Scaling Ceiling** | Scales to millions of records | Sweet spot up to ~30k to 50k records; past that, shard by continent or move to a Web Worker + inverted index | #### Trade-Off 2: Building a Custom Structured Markdown CMS Instead of Using Decap CMS The old repo used **Decap CMS** ([content/source-repo/admin/config.yml](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/content/source-repo/admin/config.yml)), which is a reasonable default for standard Markdown blogs. The trouble showed up the moment you opened a **15,505-line** file like [italy.md](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/content/saints/regions/italy.md) in a generic WYSIWYG editor: nested bullet indentation got mangled, the author's handwritten parentheticals disappeared, and the browser DOM slowed to a crawl. **What I ended up building instead:** I wrote a custom dual-mode **Structured Editor** ([StructuredEditor.tsx](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/components/StructuredEditor/StructuredEditor.tsx)) backed by a domain-specific parser and serializer ([regionsParser.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/utils/regionsParser.ts), [regionsSerializer.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/utils/regionsSerializer.ts)): - **Lossless Fallback Pattern:** Whenever a line doesn't fit the standard template (say, a multi-sentence archival note or a personal travel observation), the parser stashes it in a `rawLine` field and writes it back verbatim on save. None of his handmade phrasing gets silently chewed up. - **GitHub-Native Auth and Concurrency:** Instead of spinning up a separate user database, [worker/index.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/worker/index.ts) handles the GitHub OAuth code exchange server-side, checks `repoData.permissions.push === true` before setting an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookie (with an 8-hour `Max-Age`), and requires the Git blob `sha` on every `PUT /api/admin/regions/:file` request so concurrent edits can't overwrite each other. - **Local Dev Parity:** [vite.config.ts](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/vite.config.ts#L20-L88) mounts an `adminApiPlugin()` Vite middleware that mirrors the exact same `/api/admin/regions` API against the local filesystem, and automatically re-runs `build-saints-index.mjs` on save so you can preview edits immediately. #### Trade-Off 3: Vite 8 SPA with Route-Level Code Splitting vs. SSR or Multi-Page HTML - **Why an SPA made sense here:** Most visitors spend their time exploring statefully, filtering across 14,290 records, switching liturgical themes, and pulling up `⌘K` search from page to page. Keeping the app as a single-page application lets `saints.json` stay warm in memory across route changes instead of starting from scratch on every click. - **Keeping the bundle disciplined:** Every secondary route (`SearchPage`, `RegionsPage`, `AdminPage`, `AboutPage`, `ContactPage`, `DonatePage`) along with `GlobalSearchModal` is lazily loaded with `React.lazy()`. Even the Markdown parser (`marked`, `11.69 KB` gzip) sits in its own chunk so someone who only visits `/home` or `/saints` never downloads it. - **Being honest about SEO:** Client-side routing updates `document.title` and `` dynamically in [App.tsx](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/src/App.tsx#L159-L168), supported by static Open Graph and Twitter Card tags in [index.html](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/index.html) and [robots.txt](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/public/robots.txt). That covers social previews and top-level indexing well enough, though if we want search engines to deeply index individual shrines and small towns, pre-rendering static route shells or generating per-region HTML snapshots at build time is the clear next step. #### Trade-Off 4: Deterministic Build Pipeline and Edge Caching - **The build chain ([package.json](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/saintstombs/blob/main/package.json#L6-L16)):** 1. `prebuild`: `node scripts/build-saints-index.mjs` regenerates `public/data/saints.json`, `public/data/filters.json`, and copies `content/saints/regions/*.md` over to `public/regions/`. 2. `tsc -b`: Runs project-referenced TypeScript builds across both the app and Node configs. 3. `vite build`: Produces content-hashed `/assets/*.js` and `/assets/*.css` bundles in `dist/`. 4. `esbuild worker/index.ts --bundle --format=esm --platform=neutral --target=esnext --outfile=dist/_worker.js`: Bundles the edge Worker into a zero-dependency `2.27 KB` gzipped module. 5. `wrangler pages deploy dist --project-name saintstombs --branch main`: Publishes static assets and `_worker.js` together to Cloudflare's edge network. - **Caching trade-offs:** Content-hashed files under `dist/assets/` can be cached immutably for as long as you want. Meanwhile, the static data files (`/data/saints.json` and `/regions/*.md`) still live at predictable, readable URLs with ETag revalidation (`W/"..."`). That trades a quick conditional `304` check for clean paths. Switching to a build-time hashed filename like `saints..json` pointed to by a tiny manifest would cut out that revalidation round trip altogether on repeat visits. --- ## 3. # Pantrie: Building a Self-Hosted Pantry & Expiration Tracker

> **Project Details**
> - **Status:** Public / Open Source (`v1.0.0`, MIT License)
> - **Launch Date:** January 20, 2026 *(v1.0.0 Self-Hosted Web Stack)* · July 20, 2026 *(Native iOS SwiftUI/SwiftData Companion Milestone)*
> - **Repository:** [github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie)
> - **Documentation:** [Full Technical Docs (README.md)](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/blob/main/README.md) · [Setup & Operations Guide (SETUP.md)](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/blob/main/SETUP.md)
> - **Release Notes & History:** [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/releases) · [Commit History](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/commits/main)
> - **Tech Stack:** Node.js 20, Express, PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, React 18, Vite, TanStack Table, Docker Compose, Caddy 2, PWA Web Push *(plus a SwiftUI / SwiftData / CloudKit iOS client)*

---

## 1. The Problem: Household Food Waste & Inventory Friction

My parents have a large pantry, and keeping track of what is actually sitting in it has always been a bit of a losing battle. Once cans, sauces, snacks, and bulk staples get pushed toward the back of deep shelves, expiration dates are easy to forget, and food ends up going to waste.

When you look closely at why that keeps happening, a few practical patterns stand out:

1. **Out of sight, out of mind:** Expiration dates are printed in tiny type on random corners of packaging, and nobody remembers them a week after unpacking groceries.
2. **Duplicate grocery runs:** Standing in a supermarket aisle, it is hard to remember whether there is already an unopened jar of marinara at home, so you buy another one while the older jar quietly expires in the back.
3. **High entry friction:** Plenty of people try tracking pantry items in a shared spreadsheet or notes app, and that makes sense on paper. In practice, typing out product names, brands, and dates for twenty items while putting away groceries gets tedious fast, and the habit usually dies within a week.
4. **Subscription fatigue:** There are commercial pantry apps on the app stores, and a few of them are pretty well designed. Still, many lock basic reminders behind monthly subscriptions, crowd the screen with ads, or keep everyday household data sitting on third-party servers that could change pricing or shut down later.

I wanted to build something my parents would actually stick with: a quiet, low-friction tool where scanning a barcode takes a few seconds, leftovers can be typed in quickly, and upcoming expirations show up before food spoils.

## 2. Who Uses It & Why Self-Hosted Docker + CLI

### Two Different Users Under One Roof

Building software for a family means designing for two very different day-to-day contexts, even inside the same house:

| User Role | Who | Where They Use It | What Matters Most |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary User (Household Member)** | Mom & Dad in the kitchen or grocery store | Mobile browser (PWA) while unpacking groceries or planning dinner | Fast camera barcode scanning, quick manual entry for produce and leftovers, a scannable expiration table, and passive morning reminders |
| **Operator / Admin** | Dad (homelab maintainer) | SSH terminal and the Admin Dashboard on his home server | Reproducible Docker Compose setup, automatic HTTPS, no random internet signups, straightforward database backups, and easy password resets |

### Why a Self-Hosted Docker & CLI Approach?

My dad already runs a homelab at home, so building Pantrie as a self-hosted Docker stack with CLI admin tooling ended up solving several headaches at once.

First up, running it on hardware that is already humming in the house means zero recurring SaaS fees and full control over the data. Backups are just standard PostgreSQL dumps on a schedule he already trusts.

Second, mobile browser security shaped the deployment model early on. For anyone who hasn't wrestled with browser camera APIs before, phones block `getUserMedia` (which the barcode scanner needs) unless the page is served over HTTPS. Bundling **Caddy 2** directly into `docker-compose.yml` handles Let's Encrypt TLS certificates automatically once a domain points to the server. That took away what is usually the most annoying step of self-hosting a camera-enabled web app.

Third, most web applications include a public `/register` page out of the box, which makes total sense for open SaaS tools. On a personal family server exposed to the public internet, though, open registration mostly invites spam accounts and extra attack surface. Leaving self-registration out and handling the first admin account (`npm run admin:create-user`) and lockout recovery (`npm run admin:reset-password`) through `docker exec` CLI commands keeps user provisioning tied to host shell access or an existing admin session. It also matches the way homelab operators already manage their services.

Finally, packaging PostgreSQL, Redis, the Node.js API, the React frontend build, and Caddy into one `docker-compose.yml` makes upgrades and server moves predictable. Pulling updates or rebuilding the stack comes down to a couple of familiar commands.

## 4. Key Features

### Expiration Alerts & Notifications
- **Daily Scheduled Check:** A `node-cron` job runs every morning at `8:00 AM` (`0 8 * * *`), comparing each user's inventory against their chosen lead time.
- **Per-User Alert Windows:** Everyone in the household can pick whether they want a heads-up **3, 7, 14, or 30 days** before items expire (`user_preferences.alert_threshold_days`).
- **Multi-Channel Delivery:** Alerts can go out as **Browser Push Notifications** (VAPID-signed `web-push` handled by the PWA Service Worker), **HTML Emails** (through `nodemailer` and any SMTP relay), or **Both**.
- **Automatic Cleanup of Stale Subscriptions:** When sending push alerts across multiple devices, the backend runs `Promise.allSettled` and deletes dead endpoints from `push_subscriptions` whenever a push service replies with HTTP `410 Gone`.
- **At-a-Glance Inventory Triage:** The main inventory table sorts by soonest expiration by default and labels every row with color-coded badges (`Expired`, `Expires Today`, warning days left, or fresh).

### Barcode Scanning & Relational Item Schema
- **Grocery-Focused Camera Scanner:** The frontend uses `html5-qrcode` aimed at the rear camera (`facingMode: 'environment'`) at `10 FPS`, narrowed specifically to **UPC-A** and **EAN-13** barcodes so the camera does not misfire on promotional QR codes printed on boxes.
- **Open Food Facts Lookup with Graceful Fallback:** For those who haven't come across it, Open Food Facts is an open, community-maintained database of grocery products. Pantrie proxies lookups through `GET /api/food-items/barcode/:barcode` with a 5-second timeout. If a product is missing, or if you are logging fresh produce and leftovers, the form keeps the scanned barcode (when present) and drops right into manual entry (`is_manual_entry: true`).
- **User-Scoped Relational Schema:** PostgreSQL stores everything across four clean tables:
  - `users` (`id`, `username`, `email`, `password_hash`, `is_admin`, `created_at`)
  - `user_preferences` (`user_id` FK, `alert_threshold_days`, `notification_method`)
  - `food_items` (`id`, `user_id` FK, `barcode` nullable, `product_name`, `brand`, `expiration_date`, `quantity`, `notes`, `is_manual_entry`, `created_at`, `updated_at`)
  - `push_subscriptions` (`id`, `user_id` FK, `endpoint`, `p256dh_key`, `auth_key`)
- **Server-Side Date Math:** Item queries calculate `EXTRACT(DAY FROM (expiration_date - CURRENT_DATE)) AS days_until_expiration` directly in PostgreSQL so expiration counts stay consistent regardless of a phone's local clock.

### CLI Commands
Account bootstrapping, cryptographic key setup, and recovery all live as interactive Node.js scripts inside the backend container:
- `npm run admin:create-user` (`backend/src/scripts/createAdmin.js`): Prompts for username, email, password, and admin status, hashes the password with bcrypt, and inserts the user plus default preferences inside a single PostgreSQL transaction.
- `npm run admin:reset-password` (`backend/src/scripts/resetPassword.js`): Looks up an account by username or email, checks the 6-character minimum length, and updates the password hash directly for quick lockout recovery.
- `npm run generate-vapid` (`backend/src/scripts/generateVapid.js`): Generates Web Push VAPID keys and prints them as copy-ready `.env` lines (`WEB_PUSH_PUBLIC_KEY`, `WEB_PUSH_PRIVATE_KEY`, `VITE_VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`).
- **Day-to-Day Ops:** Paired with standard `docker-compose` lifecycle commands and one-line `pg_dump` / `psql` backup and restore workflows.

### Container Architecture
- **Five Services on an Isolated Network:** `pantrie-postgres`, `pantrie-redis`, `pantrie-backend`, `pantrie-frontend`, and `pantrie-caddy` talk over a dedicated `pantrie-network` bridge.
- **Healthcheck-Gated Startup:** `pantrie-backend` waits until both PostgreSQL (`pg_isready`) and Redis (`redis-cli ping`) report healthy before booting, and exposes its own `/health` endpoint checked every 30 seconds.
- **Static-Only Frontend Image:** `pantrie-frontend` builds the Vite bundle inside `node:20-alpine`, copies `/app/dist` into a `FROM scratch` image, and shares it with Caddy through the `frontend-dist` volume. That avoids running a separate Nginx or Node server just to serve static assets.
- **Edge Hardening via Caddy:** Caddy handles automatic HTTPS (including HTTP/3 QUIC on UDP 443), compresses responses with `gzip` and `zstd`, writes JSON access logs, removes the `Server` header, and sets `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy`, and a Content Security Policy allowlisting `world.openfoodfacts.org`.

### Persistence Layer
- **Named Volumes for Clean Upgrades:** Five Docker volumes keep persistent state separate from container rebuilds: `postgres-data` for the relational database, `redis-data` for Redis 7 with Append-Only File persistence (`--appendonly yes`), `frontend-dist` for built assets, and `caddy-data` / `caddy-config` for ACME certificates and proxy state.
- **Automated Backups:** Set up to work cleanly with a nightly host cron job (`0 2 * * * docker exec pantrie-postgres pg_dump ... | gzip`) and plain SQL restores.
- **Phase 2 Native iOS Expansion:** Since then, in July 2026, I added a native SwiftUI companion app (`Pantrie/`) backed by **SwiftData and CloudKit** sync, local `UNUserNotificationCenter` alerts, storage location tags (`Pantry`, `Fridge`, `Freezer`), and automatic food category inference from Open Food Facts v2.

## 5. Engineering Decisions & Trade-Offs

To dig into how the system was actually built, here is a summary of the main technical choices and why I landed on them.

| Area | What I Chose | Why It Made Sense Here |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Language & Runtime** | Node.js 20 (native ESM) + Express, React 18 + Vite | Sharing JavaScript across the API, PWA frontend, and admin CLI scripts kept context-switching low while giving access to mature packages (`pg`, `web-push`, `node-cron`, `html5-qrcode`). |
| **Database** | PostgreSQL 16 with parameterized SQL via `pg.Pool` | Foreign keys, ACID transactions, native date arithmetic, and reliable `pg_dump` backups beat out SQLite once multi-user isolation and concurrent web plus cron jobs were in the picture. |
| **Auth & Access Control** | Stateless Passport JWT + bcrypt (10 rounds) + admin-only user creation | Keeps mobile PWA auth simple without sticky sessions; every item query filters by `user_id` to prevent cross-user access; `helmet` and `express-rate-limit` (100 req / 15 min) protect `/api/`. |
| **Docker & Compose** | Alpine images, non-root `nodejs` user (`UID 1001`), `FROM scratch` frontend | Keeps images lean, avoids running the API as `root`, and lets Caddy pull double duty as TLS terminator and static file host. |
| **Error Handling** | Centralized Express error middleware + PostgreSQL SQLSTATE mapping | Turns database errors (`23505` to `409 Conflict`, `23503` to `400 Bad Request`) into consistent JSON responses while hiding raw stack details in production. |
| **Testing & Verification** | Joi boundary validation, container healthchecks, and a manual setup checklist | Got a working v1 into my parents' kitchen quickly, with a clear plan for adding automated unit, integration, and CI tests next. |

### Language & Full-Stack Coherence
For a solo self-hosted project, keeping the API, operational CLI scripts, Service Worker, and React UI in one language saved a lot of friction. Express stays out of the way and keeps routes easy to read, while Vite and TanStack Table give the inventory page a quick, spreadsheet-like feel (search, column sorting, filtering) without pulling in a heavy UI suite.

Meanwhile, building the Phase 2 SwiftUI client showed where native platforms still shine over web apps: camera launch is snappier, SwiftData works offline naturally, and iOS local notifications do not need an SMTP server or VAPID key management.

### Database & Query Safety
ORMs like Prisma or Sequelize are popular in Node projects, and they are pretty good when you are juggling dozens of tables and complex migrations. For a four-table schema, though, adding an ORM felt like extra abstraction I did not need. Writing raw parameterized SQL (`$1`, `$2`, ...) directly with `pg.Pool` protects against SQL injection, keeps every query transparent when debugging, and makes PostgreSQL features like `EXTRACT(DAY FROM ...)` trivial to use.

Every `food_items` read, update, and delete includes `WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2` so one household member cannot accidentally or intentionally touch another user's records by guessing an integer ID. On top of that, creating a user (in both `POST /api/admin/users` and `createAdmin.js`) wraps the `users` insert and the default `user_preferences` insert in an explicit `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` transaction with `ROLLBACK` and `client.release()` in a `finally` block. That way, an account never lands in the database half-configured.

One honest architectural note: `redis:7-alpine` with AOF persistence is wired into `docker-compose.yml` (`REDIS_URL`) to support future Open Food Facts barcode caching and JWT revocation, while v1 runs authentication statelessly via Passport JWT to stay simple.

### Dockerfile & Compose Design
A few small container hygiene choices make a big difference in a homelab stack:
- `backend/Dockerfile` installs production packages only (`npm ci --only=production`), creates an unprivileged `nodejs` user (`UID/GID 1001`), updates ownership on `/app`, and switches off root with `USER nodejs`.
- `frontend/Dockerfile` compiles the Vite bundle using build-time `ARG VITE_API_URL`, then drops everything except `/app/dist` into `FROM scratch`. Mounted into `pantrie-caddy` via the shared `frontend-dist` volume, the frontend uses practically no runtime memory.
- `docker-compose.yml` gates backend startup on `condition: service_healthy` for Postgres and Redis so the API does not crash-loop during first boot. Inside `backend/src/index.js`, `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` handlers let the server exit cleanly during `docker-compose down`.
- Separate `.dockerignore` files in `backend/` and `frontend/` keep `node_modules/`, `.env*` secrets, logs, and `dist/` out of the Docker build context.

### Error Handling & External Dependencies
At the API edge, `backend/src/middleware/validation.js` validates payloads with Joi using `{ abortEarly: false }`, returning all field errors together in one `400` response instead of making the user fix one field at a time. Downstream, `backend/src/middleware/errorHandler.js` maps PostgreSQL constraint errors (`23505` for unique conflicts, `23503` for missing foreign keys) to clean HTTP status codes and strips raw error messages whenever `NODE_ENV` is not `development`.

External APIs are where kitchen apps usually break down, so barcode lookup was written to fail softly. Open Food Facts is a community database and can be slow or missing local store brands. The backend caps requests at `5000` ms and returns `{ found: false }` on timeouts or misses instead of throwing a `500`. In `AddItemPage.jsx`, that automatically preserves the scanned barcode and opens the manual entry fields so unpacking groceries never stalls.

Notification delivery follows the same mindset. If SMTP credentials or VAPID keys are left blank in `.env`, `notificationService.js` logs a warning and skips that channel rather than crashing the daily cron job. Multi-device Web Push delivery uses `Promise.allSettled` so one expired browser subscription never blocks alerts to another phone.

### CLI Ergonomics & Developer Experience
I skipped heavy CLI frameworks and built the admin scripts directly on Node's built-in `readline` module. They stay small, have zero extra dependencies, and focus on clear prompts: sensible defaults (`Is Admin? (yes/no) [yes]`), plain validation messages, proper exit codes (`0` vs `1`), and readable `✓` confirmation summaries. `npm run generate-vapid` prints exact `.env` assignments so setup is a straight copy-and-paste.

On the documentation side, I split the docs into two pieces on purpose: [README.md](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/blob/main/README.md) as the full technical reference (endpoints, schema, security, backups) and [SETUP.md](https://github.com/ryanrclewis/pantrie/blob/main/SETUP.md) as a step-by-step deployment and troubleshooting guide alongside `.env.example`.

### Testing & Verification
For the initial homelab release, I leaned on runtime guardrails and structured manual checks rather than building out an automated test suite upfront. Specifically, v1 relies on Joi request validation, PostgreSQL foreign-key and unique constraints, Docker healthchecks across Postgres, Redis, and the API, and a 9-step verification checklist in `SETUP.md` covering container health, migrations, admin login, user creation, barcode and manual item entry, and notification settings.

Being upfront about that trade-off matters: there are no automated unit or integration tests in the repository yet. Before pushing Pantrie toward wider community use, the next step is putting a straightforward test setup in place:
1. **Unit tests (Vitest or Node's built-in test runner):** Covering expiration-day boundary math (`days < 0`, `days === 0`, threshold edges), alert text formatting, and Joi schema validation.
2. **API integration tests (Supertest + ephemeral PostgreSQL via Testcontainers):** Verifying JWT auth, cross-user isolation (`404`/`403`), transaction rollbacks on duplicate emails (`409`), and mocked Open Food Facts timeouts.
3. **GitHub Actions CI:** Running `docker-compose config` checks, container build checks, and clean schema migration smoke tests on every commit.

## 7. What I Learned & What's Next

Two lessons stuck with me while putting Pantrie together. First, browser security rules can quietly dictate your whole infrastructure. Realizing early on that phones block camera scanning without HTTPS turned automatic TLS with Caddy from a nice bonus into a core piece of the architecture. Second, designing the fallback path matters just as much as the happy path. No barcode database covers local bakery bread, farmers' market produce, or last night's soup, so making manual entry feel quick and natural kept the app usable in a real kitchen.

Going forward, there are a few clear pieces I want to clean up and build next:
1. Commit the SQL migration file (`backend/migrations/01_init.sql`) and wire up `npm run migrate` so anyone cloning the repo gets a clean database setup out of the box.
2. Put the provisioned Redis container to work caching `/api/food-items/barcode/:barcode` responses to cut repeat lookup latency and avoid leaning too hard on Open Food Facts.
3. Add shared household inventories so both of my parents can view and edit one shared pantry while keeping their own alert preferences, alongside automated Vitest and Supertest checks in CI.
